standard.title: Ethical and sustainable food and fibre enterprises
standard.description: analyse and make judgements on the ethical, secure and sustainable production and marketing of food and fibre enterprises
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can analyse how food and fibre are produced in managed environments and how food and fibre production systems are affected by innovation and sustainability requirements (AC9TDE8K04). They can identify production methods and sustainability considerations. They have not yet made judgements on ethics and security in production and marketing, nor analysed food and water security, digital production tools, or marketing chain impacts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse and make judgements on the ethical, secure and sustainable production and marketing of food and fibre enterprises — including production technology choices, environmental interdependencies, food security, and the marketing chain.

nodes.label: Emerging production technologies and methods
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse emerging production technologies in terms of productivity, profitability and sustainability, including their ethical implications.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe one emerging production technology or method (e.g. protected cropping, hydroponics, aquaculture) and identify one productivity benefit and one sustainability or ethical consideration.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse emerging production technologies and methods — protected cropping, hydroponics, aquaculture, precision livestock systems — evaluating productivity, profitability and sustainability for each; include animal welfare considerations where relevant; explain how different production systems involve different trade-offs.
wider: Analyse grain sources used by First Nations Australians (e.g. acacia) for their nutrient content and suitability as sustainable food sources in drought-prone regions — compare with conventional cereal crops for productivity and sustainability

Investigate precision agriculture tools (GPS tracking, crop sensors, automated feeding, drones for weed management) and evaluate how digital technologies change the ethics and sustainability profile of production systems
Compare intensive and extensive production systems for a specific animal product — evaluate environmental impact, animal welfare and productivity trade-offs

response_modes.reason: Production technology trade-offs look different across production types — crop-based systems have different ethical and sustainability tensions than livestock systems, and digital tools introduce different considerations again. Multiple contexts build a more complete analytical picture than a single production type.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The First Nations grains direction is substantive — it inverts the conventional framing of 'emerging technology' and reveals sustainable production knowledge that predates contemporary agriculture, which is analytically rich.
success_criteria: Identifies a specific production technology and correctly assesses at least one sustainability or ethical consideration
Goes beyond description — makes a comparative or evaluative judgement about the technology's implications

nodes.label: Environmental interdependencies in production
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse the interdependence of plants and animals in food and fibre systems and compare the environmental impacts of different production approaches.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe one example of environmental interdependence in a food or fibre production system; explain how a production decision affects that interdependence.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse the interdependence of plants and animals in production systems — including the impact of pesticide use on non-target species (e.g. bees), comparison of caged vs free-range production, and how production choices cascade through ecosystems; make a judgement about the most sustainable approach given the trade-offs.
wider: Investigate the impact of pesticide use on bee populations in a specific agricultural context — evaluate how the production benefit compares to the ecosystem cost and what alternatives exist
Analyse how food and water security concerns — including water-efficient irrigation and protected cropping — shape production decisions for preferred futures
Compare two production systems for the same product that differ in their environmental footprint — judge which is more sustainable and under what conditions the other approach might be justified
success_criteria: Identifies a specific environmental interdependency in a food or fibre system
Analyses how a production decision affects the interdependency — not just states both separately

nodes.label: Marketing chains and ethical trade
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine the marketing chain of agricultural products and analyse the effect of processing, advertising and cash crop dynamics on price, demand and communities.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two stages in the marketing chain of an agricultural product; explain how processing or marketing at one stage affects price or demand.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse the marketing chain of a range of agricultural products — from production through processing, distribution and retail to consumer; explain how product processing and advertising affect demand and price; examine the impact of cash crops on communities, including who benefits and who bears risk.
wider: Trace the full marketing chain of a specific agricultural product (e.g. coffee, cotton, cacao) and make a judgement on where ethical trade practices are and aren't present
Examine how food labelling (including country of origin, fair trade, organic) affects consumer decisions and producer pricing — evaluate how effective labelling is as an ethical tool
Investigate the impact of a cash crop economy on a specific community — analyse how dependence on a single export crop affects food security and economic resilience

response_modes.reason: Marketing chain analysis requires students to trace value and decision-making across multiple actors — producers, processors, distributors, retailers, consumers. Without a structured chain-tracing approach, students focus on production and ignore downstream dynamics that determine who benefits and who bears risk.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Full marketing chain tracing for a global commodity (coffee, cotton) is rich because the ethics are multi-layered — price volatility, fair trade certification, processing value-add, and consumer labelling all interact in ways that require genuine analytical work.
success_criteria: Identifies at least two distinct stages in a marketing chain
Explains how a decision at one stage affects price, demand or community outcomes at another
